subtype: Approach: insisting on copying a friend's grand party [Pitfall]
passage: I'm Rehana, and I live next door to Shankar. On Monday at recess he told everyone about a classmate's party with a magician and a huge bouncy castle. "Mine will be exactly like that," he said. On Tuesday, through the wall, I heard his father say it was too much for the family. Shankar shut his door hard and skipped dinner. On Wednesday he sat on the stairs, staring, and said nothing about the party for two days. Then I saw him drawing on an old calendar page: cricket in the lane, a big chocolate cake, everyone's names. "This is what I actually like," he told me.

qa.q: What did Shankar want at his party?
qa.a: Shankar wanted a bouncy castle and a magician like a classmate's party.

qa.q: What was Shankar feeling after his father said it was too much for the family?
qa.a: Shankar was upset and disappointed; shutting the door hard, skipping dinner and staring silently on the stairs all point to it. 😔

qa.q: What alternative approach could Shankar use, and why?
qa.a: Shankar could start with what he enjoys and what the family can afford, and then add one special touch. A plan that fits the family means less arguing and more fun.

qa.q: How does Rehana see what happens to Shankar?
qa.a: Rehana watches from next door and hears the argument, so Rehana sees a neighbour go from sulking to planning and seems relieved when Shankar shares the drawing.

grounding: A boy insists on copying a classmate's grand party, the family cannot afford it and he is upset until he plans around his own favourites.

subtype: Approach: insisting on copying a friend's grand party [Pitfall]
passage:
Monday. Pankaj came home from his classmate's party glowing. "A magician AND a bouncy castle! I want the same." His mother, Irawati, went quiet and said they'd talk.
Wednesday. They talked. The castle and the magician cost more than the family could manage. Pankaj slammed his door. "Then I don't want any party." He didn't come out for dinner.
Saturday. Up on the roof with his kite, Pankaj forgot to sulk long enough to notice he was happy. He thought: what do I actually like? Kites. Friends. Samosas. He ran downstairs. "Amma, can my party be a kite party on the roof?"

qa.q: What did Pankaj's classmate have at the party?
qa.a: A bouncy castle and a magician.

qa.q: How did Pankaj feel on Wednesday?
qa.a: He felt upset and disappointed, slamming his door and refusing any party at all.

qa.q: What changed Pankaj's plan, and why did it help?
qa.a: Thinking about what he actually likes, kites, friends and samosas, instead of copying his classmate; it gave him a party that fits the family.

qa.q: How might Irawati have felt through the week?
qa.a: Irawati went quiet on Monday and faced a slammed door on Wednesday, so she likely felt sad, then relieved when he asked for a kite party.

grounding: Shows a boy insisting on a classmate's grand party, feeling upset when the family cannot afford it, until he thinks about what he enjoys.

subtype: Approach: insisting on copying a friend's grand party [Pitfall]
passage: Tanvir, you're sulking because your friend had a magician? Sit. Your Thomas Uncle once did exactly the same. I was nine, in Kochi, and a classmate had a party with a magician who pulled a pigeon out of a hat, and a bouncy castle too. I went home and demanded both. My father, a bus conductor then, looked at the floor and said we couldn't. I cried, I refused my dinner, I said I'd have no party at all. Then my grandmother asked me, 'What do you like doing? You, not your classmate.' I said, 'Fishing in the backwaters, and football.' So my party was fishing off the jetty with four friends, and fried fish after. I still remember every fish.

qa.q: What did the magician pull out of a hat?
How did young Thomas feel when his father said they couldn't?
qa.a: Young Thomas was upset and disappointed; he cried, refused dinner and said he'd have no party at all.

qa.q: What choice in the story turned things around?
qa.a: Answering his grandmother's question about what he himself liked, which led to a fishing party he still remembers.

qa.q: How might Thomas's father have felt saying no?
qa.a: He looked at the floor, so he probably felt sad and a little ashamed that he couldn't give his son what the classmate had.

grounding: Illustrates a boy demanding a classmate's grand party, being upset when the family cannot afford it, and finding joy in what he himself enjoys.
